![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223877/assets/cece4e226becb315d6d951a8ae782750da79209d9a67ec52a8cd4d134999e9e6.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,z(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $4$ whose base is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,z(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223877/assets/21e29d99d2d5330db2d946d981e4bd0f820ce26297bf95f962cb3000f0998136.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=4$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=4$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,z(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,4(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =4(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}4(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S \\  & =4{∬}_{D}4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{∬}_{D}4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =4{∬}_{D}(4-{r}^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}4r-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}4r-{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =4\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[2{r}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =8\pi \cdot (18-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =-18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,0(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =-18\pi +0 \\  & =-18\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨0,\,0,\,z{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $3$ whose base is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $z$-component of $F=⟨0,\,0,\,z{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral side of $S$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the top and bottom sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223877/assets/7f44bc35687020594b0d26a2e25b9dbd2b8d75c964a90184626afad6afc1b1e8.png)

 
Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the top surface. On this surface, we have $z=3$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨0,\,0,\,z{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,3{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =3{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}3{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying a change of variables $(x,y)\to (r,\theta ),\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{D}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =3\cdot 2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{r}^{2}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3\pi (e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the bottom surface. On this surface, we have $z=0$ for ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$ Therefore, for everywhere on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
F(x,y,0)=⟨0,\,0,\,0{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =3\pi (e-1)+0 \\  & =3\pi (e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223877/assets/6bd0ac15180df7a413691a1f1f15980b47e88c63e1d3af914175231c172ca97c.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x-y,\,y+x,\,z⟩$ and the boundary $S$ of a spherical solid of radius $3$ centered at the origin. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=3.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{3}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

Using the fact that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x-y,\,y+x,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x-y,\,y+x,\,z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(x(x-y)+y(y+x)+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}-xy+{y}^{2}+xy+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}3\,\text{d}S \\  & =3{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =3\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =3\cdot 4\pi \cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =108\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For a sphere or radius $r$ centered at $O,$ the unit normal to the sphere is given by

$$
n=\frac{⟨x,y,z⟩}{r}.
$$

In our case, we have $r=3.$ Therefore,

$$
n=\frac{1}{3}⟨x,y,z⟩.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x{z}^{2},\,0,\,-{x}^{2}z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x{z}^{2},\,0,\,-{x}^{2}z⟩\cdot ⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({x}^{2}{z}^{2}+0-{x}^{2}{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0\end{aligned}

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of the rectangular solid shown above in the first octant. Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that only the $x$-component of $F=⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩$ is non-zero. Since the lateral sides of $S$ are parallel to the $x$-axis, the flux of $F$ through $S$ will be non-zero only at the front and back sides. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14223877/assets/dc37a067eb8070ecbdfea53c1ede3e221e1873a192b50fcbf07234f33c183787.png)

  

Let's consider the flux of $F$ through these two sides.

- Let ${S}_{1}$ denote the front surface. On this surface, we have $x=3$ for $0\le y\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{1}$ is

$$
{n}_{1}=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=3$ on ${S}_{1},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{1} & =⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨12{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{1}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}12{y}^{2}{z}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[4{y}^{3}{z}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[8{z}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- Let ${S}_{2}$ denote the back surface. On this surface, we have $x=0$ for $0\le y\le 2$ and $0\le z\le 1.$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector to ${S}_{2}$ is

$$
{n}_{2}=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $x=0$ on ${S}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot {n}_{2} & =⟨4x{y}^{2}{z}^{3},\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across ${S}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}0\,\text{d}S \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
